blocks.label: Paragraph · The config is where the run is actually shaped. Its defaults ar…
blocks.md: The config is where the run is actually shaped. Its defaults are sane, but the training block is the part worth understanding — and the part worth experimenting with.

blocks.label: Paragraph · A config has four sections: audio, model, training and inferenc…
blocks.md: A config has four sections: `audio`, `model`, `training` and `inference`. You rarely touch the first two, with one exception: the audio chunk size. Which block owns the rest of the spectrum settings — `n_fft`, `hop_length`, `dim_f` — depends on the architecture, and there is a [table of who owns what](#hop-length-a-property-of-the-model-not-a-taste) below the calculator.

blocks.label: Subheading · chunk_size — the one audio setting you will change
blocks.md: chunk\_size — the one audio setting you will change

blocks.label: Paragraph · The trainer reads the window itself from audio.chunk_size, in s…
blocks.md: The trainer reads the window itself from `audio.chunk_size`, in samples — that key is the one every architecture family reads. Configs also describe the same window in frames (`dim_t`), and because every STFT here runs with `center=True` the two are one value in two units:

blocks.label: Label · The formula
blocks.md: The formula

blocks.label: Paragraph · chunk_size = (dim_t − 1) × hop_length
blocks.md: `chunk_size = (dim_t − 1) × hop_length`

blocks.label: Paragraph · The conversions above assume hop_length: 441 — the step every p…
blocks.md: The conversions above assume `hop_length: 441` — the step every published Roformer in this guide uses. A different hop gives a different sample count for the same `dim_t`, because the frame count is what follows from the window: `floor(chunk_size ÷ hop_length) + 1`. So the hop decides both the window and the memory, and it belongs to the model rather than to you — the [hop\_length section](#hop-length-a-property-of-the-model-not-a-taste) below the calculator has the details. Smaller chunks train faster and use less VRAM; larger chunks teach the model longer musical context. This is the main dial you change when a run will not fit.

blocks.label: Label · Schematic · chunk windows drawn to scale
blocks.md: Schematic · chunk windows drawn to scale

blocks.label: Caption · The one audio setting worth changing. Roformer and MDX-Net conf…
blocks.md: The one audio setting worth changing. Roformer and MDX-Net configs describe their window in frames (`dim_t`); the trainer reads samples (`chunk_size`). Bars are scaled to a 16-second excerpt, so what you are looking at is how much musical context each setting sees.

blocks.label: Subheading · hop_length and n_fft — which block of the config owns them
blocks.md: hop\_length and n\_fft — which block of the config owns them

blocks.label: Paragraph · hop_length is the step between STFT frames, and it is not a fre…
blocks.md:
`hop_length` is the step between STFT frames, and it is not a free preference: it is baked into the
        spectrogram the weights were trained on, so change it and the checkpoint you are fine-tuning no longer matches its
        own input. Where you change it, though, depends on the architecture — and this is the mistake that costs people an
        afternoon, because a Roformer config and an mdx23c config both have an `n_fft` and a
        `hop_length`, in *different blocks*, and only one of the two counts in each.

blocks.label: Paragraph · The mechanism is plain in the source. mel_band_roformer and bs_…
blocks.md:
The mechanism is plain in the source. `mel_band_roformer` and `bs_roformer` are constructed as
        `MelBandRoformer(**config.model)`, and SCNet as `SCNet(**config.model)` — the model block is
        the only thing they see, and their STFT parameters are named there. mdx23c and DTTNet go the other way and are
        handed the whole audio block (`STFT(config.audio)`), so for them `audio.n_fft`,
        `audio.hop_length` and `audio.dim_f` are the real ones. What every family reads from
        `audio` is `chunk_size`, `num_channels`, `sample_rate` and
        `min_mean_abs`.

Two rules account for every config in this ecosystem, and which one is right depends entirely on where your config
        came from:

blocks.label: Paragraph · Every published Roformer checkpoint this guide tells you to fin…
blocks.md:
Every *published* Roformer checkpoint this guide tells you to fine-tune uses `441` — a tenth of
        the sample rate, so a frame lands exactly on 10 ms of audio at any full-band rate. The blank templates that ship with
        MSST, and the DTTNet config, use `n_fft ÷ 4` — the ordinary 75 % overlap you would pick for a fresh STFT —
        and mdx23c halves that again. So “keep `hop_length = n_fft ÷ 4`” is good advice for a config you are
        writing from scratch and the wrong advice for a checkpoint you are continuing: load Kimberley Jensen's model with
        `hop_length: 512` and its learned features no longer line up with the input you feed them.

That is why the calculator's hop rule is a choice rather than a constant, and why it carries an `n_fft`
        field: both STFT rules are measured from the window, and `dim_f` — the width the transformer actually
        reads — is half of it, so `n_fft: 2048` is `dim_f: 1024`, `4096` is `2048`.
        A wider window is therefore also a wider spectrogram and a heavier model, which is the one part of the memory
        estimate the calculator still does not scale for.

blocks.label: Label · Don't tune the copy that is ignored
blocks.md: Don't tune the copy that is ignored

blocks.label: Paragraph · A Roformer config carries hop_length twice — once under audio…
blocks.md:
A Roformer config carries `hop_length` twice — once under `audio`, once as
            `model.stft_hop_length` — and the shipped ones annotate the first copy `# don't work (use in model)`. viperx's BS-Roformer config says exactly that about both `audio.hop_length: 441` and
            `audio.dim_t: 801`. For mdx23c and DTTNet there is no second copy to get wrong: edit
            `audio.hop_length` or edit nothing. Setting both copies to the same number keeps a config readable
            either way.

blocks.label: Paragraph · Because the hop decides how many frames the window divides into…
blocks.md:
Because the hop decides how many frames the window divides into, and the frame count is what the model attends
        over, the hop is a memory setting as much as a spectral one. At a fixed `chunk_size` the relationship is
        exact: `frames = floor(chunk_size ÷ hop_length) + 1`, so `chunk_size: 587412` is 1333 frames
        at `hop_length: 441` and 1148 frames at `512` — the same 13.3 seconds of audio, seen through
        far fewer, wider steps. That is the direction the calculator's hop rule moves in: it holds the window and lets the
        frame count follow. Run it the other way — hold `dim_t` and let the window grow — and
        `dim_t: 801` is an 8.00 s window at `441` but a 9.29 s one at `512`. Which of the
        two you want depends on what you are doing: keeping `chunk_size` is how you switch conventions without
        changing the music the model hears, and keeping `dim_t` is what a fine-tune does when it inherits the
        frames its checkpoint was trained on.

blocks.label: Subheading · Sample rate — the band each choice keeps
blocks.md: Sample rate — the band each choice keeps

blocks.label: Paragraph · The sample rate is not a memory dial, but it does decide someth…
blocks.md:
The sample rate is not a memory dial, but it does decide something you cannot undo later: everything above
        *half* the rate — the Nyquist frequency — is gone before training starts. A rate of 22 050 Hz keeps
        0–11 025 Hz and throws away cymbals, sibilance and guitar harmonics: free for a bass model, fatal for a drum
        model.

blocks.label: Paragraph · Halving the rate halves what the loader reads and what the STFT…
blocks.md:
Halving the rate halves what the loader reads and what the STFT transforms, and whether it halves
        the memory depends entirely on the hop — because `frames = chunk_size ÷ hop_length + 1`. At a fixed
        `chunk_size` a halved rate makes the same chunk *twice as long*, so you get twice the frames and the
        estimate doubles; halve `chunk_size` at the same time and it comes straight back to where it started.
        That is exactly what `hop_length = rate ÷ 100` arranges without you thinking about it:
        `frames per second = rate ÷ hop_length` is 100 at every full-band rate, so the frame count follows the
        seconds of audio and nothing else. Under a fixed hop it does not: at `hop_length: 512` a halved rate
        halves the frames per second, so the same 13.3 s window arrives as 574 frames instead of 1148 — half the memory, and
        each frame now steps 23.2 ms instead of 11.6 ms. One arithmetic wrinkle, and only under the
        `rate ÷ 100` rule: 22 050 ÷ 100 is not a whole number, so the hop lands on 221 rather than 220.5 —
        10.02 ms per frame instead of 10, which moves the window by tens of milliseconds — while 24 000 ÷ 100 = 240 lands
        exactly. Switch the rule to `n_fft ÷ 4` and the wrinkle disappears: `512` at any rate.

blocks.label: Label · A halved rate is an experiment, not a setting
blocks.md: A halved rate is an experiment, not a setting

blocks.label: Paragraph · No model in this guide's ecosystem is published below 44.1 kHz…
blocks.md:
No model in this guide's ecosystem is published below 44.1 kHz, and the mel filterbank is built *from*
            the sample rate — change the rate and a checkpoint's learned features no longer line up with the input they are
            being fed. If you try it, change `audio.sample_rate`, `audio.hop_length` and the
            `sample_rate` in the `loss_multistft` block together, then judge the run on validation
            metrics against an untouched full-band baseline.

blocks.label: Subheading · Channels — stereo is architecture, not file format
blocks.md: Channels — stereo is architecture, not file format

blocks.label: Paragraph · Every Roformer published for this ecosystem is stereo, and the…
blocks.md:
Every Roformer published for this ecosystem is stereo, and the config says so twice: `audio.num_channels: 2`
        and `model.stereo: true`. Those lines describe the *model*, not your files. The band-split front end
        turns each mel band's two channels into one longer sequence for the transformer to attend over, which is why a
        stereo run costs more than a mono one — and why the calculator now asks which you are training.

The distinction matters in both directions. If your source material is mono, you have not made training any
        cheaper: a stereo model still expects two channels, so the mono file arrives duplicated. And if you genuinely want
        a mono model, you change the architecture — `num_channels: 1` together with `stereo: false`,
        trained on mono mixtures and targets — which halves the sequence and so most of the activation memory.

blocks.label: Label · Mono is a different model, not a smaller version of the same one
blocks.md: Mono is a different model, not a smaller version of the same one

blocks.label: Paragraph · A checkpoint trained with stereo: true will not load into a ste…
blocks.md:
A checkpoint trained with `stereo: true` will not load into a `stereo: false` model — the
            shapes differ, so you are training from scratch, not fine-tuning. Mono suits material that is genuinely
            single-channel (a bass DI, a close-mic drum, a mono room recording) and is a bad deal wherever the stereo image
            carries information: wide guitars, spacious drums, reverb tails. Judge it on the same validation metrics as any
            other architecture change.
